newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK trade gap shrinks despite soaring pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK trade gap shrinks despite soaring pound.

text.p: Britain's trade gap with the rest of the world narrowed sharply in May but the country's top business lobby warned the improvement would be short-lived with export orders tumbling under the strain of the soaring pound.
The Office for National Statistics said on Thursday Britain's global trade gap totalled 508 million pounds ($851.2 million) in May, down from 989 million in April.

But the Confederation of British Industry's (CBI) quarterly industrial trends survey found export orders in the four months to July fell at their fastest rate since late 1991, when Britain was mired in the longest recession since World War Two.
In stark contrast, the CBI said domestic demand rose faster than at any time since April 1995 over the latest four months.

"The survey results clearly show a sharp dichotomy in the economy with domestic demand continuing to grow, while export orders and confidence...are being hit by the strength of sterling," said Andrew Buxton, chairman of the CBI's economic affairs committee and Barclays Bank.

The pound has climbed relentlessly since last August and has now gained more than 25 percent against a basket of major currencies. As it rises, it pushes up exporters' prices, making it tougher to sell goods abroad.
Earlier this week, after retail sales were shown to have leapt in June, chalking up the highest quarterly growth rate since 1988, the pound stormed to an eight-year high of nearly 3.09 German marks.

The CBI's survey is two months more up to date than the ONS figures but it has been trumpeting manufacturers' concerns about sterling for months while the official data has shown healthy export growth.
Economists said many firms have been trying to compensate for the high pound by hedging currency positions, cutting prices and sometimes their profit margins to sell their goods abroad.
"But that can't last indefinitely. It would be a major shock if the trade figures don't show real signs of damage in the last few months of the year," Philip Shaw, economist at Investec Bank, said.
Not only does a sky-high pound cut export sales, it also makes imported goods cheaper on Britain's high streets -- a double whammy for the trade balance.
More up-to-date figures covering trade with countries outside the European Union countries may already be starting to show the strain of the pound's rally, even though the global figures do not.
Britain's non-EU trade deficit swelled to 713 million pounds in June, from 584 million in May, the ONS said. Exports fell 1.4 percent while imports rose 0.5 percent.

"We are likely to see this trend of falling export volumes and rising import volumes continuing in the coming months," said James McKay, economist at PaineWebber. "Sterling is certainly starting to take its toll and its going to get a lot worse later in the year."

British industrialists wholeheartedly agreed. Buxton at the CBI said the Bank of England should think long and hard before raising interest rates again soon, as that would probably push the pound higher still.

But he admitted the strength of consumer demand left Britain's new Monetary Policy Committee with a thorny dilemma. It meets next on August 6 and 7. Base rates have been ratcheted up in quarter-point moves three times since May to 6.75 percent. ($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
